A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same speculative-sampling research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-mixture, CIFAR-10, LSUN, latent-diffusion, and PushT experiments in Section 6 and Appendix J.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds acceleration-method comparisons, parallel-sampling experiments, and a phi-4 Langevin simulation in Appendices J and K.

M1.justification: Appendix B adds an efficient frozen-draft variant that reuses previously computed verification drifts, changing proposal construction after rejection. Section 5 and Algorithm 11 additionally specialize speculative sampling to ULA with proxy-energy or frozen-gradient drafts. The original reflection coupling and Picard-based drafting were already present in v1.

E1.justification: Appendix K adds sampling from an unnormalized phi-4 energy model on an 8-by-8 grid, extending evaluation into physical-system MCMC. The Gaussian-mixture, image-generation, latent CIFAR-10, and PushT coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's draft and target comparisons, v2 Table 3 evaluates uniform, EDM, and learned LD3 timestep schedules and multistep moment-matching distillation. It separately includes published DPM-Solver++ results with naive, AYS, and LD3 schedules. Table 9 adds ordinary Langevin sampling as the comparator for the new application.

E3.justification: Appendix J introduces a 30-step CIFAR-10 combination experiment, selecting the best FID over window sizes 5, 10, and 20, plus approximately 15-NFE baseline comparisons. Appendix K adds a 100,000-step ULA protocol with stepsize 0.001 and speculative window 20. These are additional protocols rather than established reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Table 8 adds a focused composability study varying parallel-call count p=0, 1, and 5 alongside temperature and stochasticity. Figure 6 adds a comparison of the acceptance-bound factor under linear and cosine schedules. Earlier temperature, dimension, and window-size analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix K newly specifies 500 runs and reports energy means and standard deviations using the last 500 simulated samples. The existing PushT episode count and uncertainty entries are unchanged; the PDFs do not establish additional repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1 Tables 1–6 are retained in v2 Tables 1, 2, and 4–7. New Tables 3 and 8 add acceleration comparisons, including hybrid CIFAR-10 FID 2.07 at 15.42 NFE with p=1, epsilon=0.25, and tau=10. Table 9 reports Langevin versus speculative NFE of 100000 versus 48564 and mean energies of 62.27 versus 65.90.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a formal counterexample showing why independently resampling from the target upon rejection is incorrect. Appendix H expands the acceptance-ratio derivation and restricts Lemma H.6 from alpha>=1 to even alpha>=2 while revising its proof constants. Section 4.1 replaces constant acceptance probability with a lower-bound assumption; the central coupling results remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit contribution concerning acceleration of Langevin sampling for unnormalized distributions. v1 contained only a general applicability remark about other discretized diffusions. The central claims of exact DDM sampling, maximal acceptance, training-free drafting, and fewer target evaluations remain.

C2.justification: The discussion adds a substantive qualification: diffusion models already exploit parallelism, so LLM-style speculative-decoding latency benefits need not transfer. Section 5 and Appendix K distinguish exact reproduction of ULA from its biased approximation to the desired density. Appendix J adds an interpretation of the combination results as evidence of complementarity.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly defines NFE as a batched target-model call regardless of batch size, labels sequential and parallel algorithm operations, and documents cached-drift initialization and reuse. It also supplies ULA pseudocode and parameters for the added experiments. Existing architecture and training details in Appendix I are largely retained.

R1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix K substantially expand positioning into MCMC prefetching, delayed acceptance, multifidelity methods, and parallel Langevin algorithms, with corresponding new references. Appendix J also establishes comparisons with AYS, LD3, and moment-matching distillation. These extend the research context beyond the retained LLM and diffusion-acceleration discussion.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose edits, standardizes draft/output notation, reorders contribution bullets, and subdivides Appendix H. It inserts a Langevin section, Appendix K, and an impact statement while retaining most of the original narrative and appendix organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds three substantive result displays—Tables 3, 8, and 9—and the schedule plot in Figure 6. Figures 2 and 3 change from side-by-side to vertically stacked panels, captions are expanded, and several displays move. The original tables and plotted results are retained rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly compared against its own draft and target samplers. v2 substantially strengthens comparative evidence through additional acceleration baselines and a direct composability study in Tables 3 and 8, while developing and testing the broader Langevin application. Its latency qualification also improves interpretation. These gains outweigh remaining limitations: the best hybrid result uses non-exact tau=10 sampling, wall-clock acceleration remains unmeasured, and Algorithm 11's rejection update prints E where Equation 38 specifies its gradient.
